blocks.cap: The Toden tram through the back streets of Kita

blocks.p: The newest knot in Gin's ledger had an address beside it, and Rei copied it onto the back of his hand. It was in Takinogawa, a quiet part of Kita west of Ōji station. In the evening he walked down to the Ōji-ekimae stop and waited for the Toden. Its platforms were no bigger than a bench, and its rails ran through back streets past houses close enough to touch. When the car came, its bell rang twice as it pulled in.

Inside, the air conditioning was weak and the windows were open. The car climbed slowly past the trees of Asukayama park, where the cicadas were so loud they drowned out the motor. An old woman sat opposite Rei with a paper bag of chrysanthemums for a grave. A boy in a baseball uniform slept with his cap over his face and his glove in his lap. Every few minutes the driver said the name of the next stop in a soft, tired voice. Rei got off at Takinogawa-itchōme and walked the rest of the way through narrow streets, past small houses with Obon lanterns by their doors and a vending machine humming alone on a corner.

The address did not go to a home. It went to a narrow building with a shuttered noodle shop on the ground floor and a stairwell that hummed. It hummed faintly, the way a transformer hums. Rei felt it as pressure in the fillings of his teeth before he heard it as sound. On the second landing someone had left a child's sandals paired neatly against the wall, the way the shoes of the dead are paired at a wake. The gift Rei always kept folded down behind his breastbone opened one degree without his permission, the way an old wound aches before rain.

By the third floor the hum had become something almost like chanting. But no one was using their voice. It was the membrane itself being made to ring, struck again and again and held. Rei felt a cold drop in his stomach. He was standing at the back door of a room where people had learned to do on purpose what he had spent his whole life trying to keep accidental.

blocks.cap: The Far-Shore Circle kneeling around their teacher

blocks.p: Through the gap of the door he saw them. Thirty people, maybe thirty-five, kneeling in seiza on cushions. Seiza is the formal way of kneeling in Japan, sitting back on the heels with the back straight, and it hurts after a while unless a person is used to it. The cushions were flat zabuton, the square floor cushions every Japanese home keeps for guests. The people were not in rows. They were in a ring, and the ring did not face a shrine or a screen or a priest. It faced inward, toward a single woman at the centre. She wore a grey summer kimono, her hands loose in her lap, her eyes closed. Every face in the circle was turned toward her, the way sunflowers turn toward the sun. It was not quite worship. It was what happens to people who have found the one source of light in a dark place.

blocks.cap: The white room in Takinogawa, the wall of the missing and the ring around the woman in grey

blocks.p: The room was white. White walls, white paper over the windows, floor cushions and nothing else. Nothing else except one wall. That wall was covered from floor to ceiling in photographs of missing people. Snapshots, school portraits, a wedding photo cut down to one face, a man on a fishing boat squinting into the sun. Some were laminated in plastic, the way posters are laminated when they are taped to station pillars in the rain. Rei knew that kind of photograph. After the tsunami of March 2011, thousands of people were never found. Their families carried photographs like these up and down the coast for months and held them up to strangers. There were hundreds here. Each one was somebody's unfinished grief, pinned where the ring could see it.

The air around the woman was doing something his eyes would not show him clearly. It shimmered like heat over asphalt. But the room was still, and the shimmer was cold. Rei had walked into more haunted rooms than he could count. He had never walked into one that was this organised about it.

Then the woman at the centre spoke, without opening her eyes and without raising her voice. She said his brother's surname, which was also his own, into the ringing quiet. In a voice of perfect hospitality she added that the seat at the eastern edge of the circle had been kept open for some time now. The tea was still warm. There was no need to keep standing in a doorway as though he were not expected. The congregation did not turn to look at him. That was the worst part. They did not need to. Whatever was looking at him was looking through all of them at once. It had been waiting, and it was pleased.
Rei took the eastern seat. Standing in the doorway would only prove he was afraid. Kneeling in the ring put him close enough to read.

He learned the shape of the room the way he learned the last hour of a drowned man. Nobody explained it to him. He read it from the thing itself. These were not believers who had come for comfort and stayed for company. They were the bereaved of a city that had too many of them. A widow whose husband had gone into the 2011 water and was never properly sent home. A mother whose son's name was on a hospital ward that no longer answered. And the young man from Sumida, the one from Gin's ledger, whose grief had been eating his sleep until something patient reached in and ate the grief instead. Each of them had carried a wound across the membrane, a thin place worn by loss. The circle did not heal those thin places. It harvested them.

The woman kneeling on his right leaned over while the ring breathed, as if they were old friends. She smelled of mothballs and menthol rub. "You're new," she whispered. "Don't worry. This is only a small one tonight."
"A small one?"
"Saturdays are the big circle." She patted his knee. "New grief arrives on Saturdays."
"How did you find it?" Rei asked.

"I didn't. Sensei found me." Her eyes were shining. "March. The memorial, on the anniversary. The fourth one, it was. There were so many people and I was at the back, I couldn't even see the stage. And a woman in grey came all the way through the crowd and took both my hands." She showed him, folding her own dry hands round his. "She said my husband's name. Before I'd said a word. How could she know that?" She let go. "Others came from the hospitals. Some from the little Tuesday circles at the community rooms. We call those the letting-go circles. Everyone is found somewhere."
She said it the way people describe being rescued. Sensei is the word for a teacher, and also for a doctor, and for anyone people look up to.

A line came back to Rei from the chapter in Gin's book about cults. He had skimmed it once, weeks ago, and thought it was jargon. A cult, stripped to its frame, is a possessed person, plus a congregation, plus a spirit operation. He had pictured robes and chanting. Here it was in a white room above a noodle shop. The possessed person at the centre. The congregation kneeling round her. And underneath them the operation, which he could feel running the way an engine is felt through a floor.

Gin had written that every congregation has two tiers, and that both must be read. Most of the ring were the first tier. They were ordinary people with no gift at all. They gave devotion, work, money and cover. They were the numbers, and a standing pool for the thing to feed on. At the worst houses, Gin had written, they were also bodies that could be offered. Most of them would never learn what sat at the centre. They had been sold a divine presence and given the comfort of belonging, and for them that was enough.

But not all of them. Rei counted four who were different. They were mediums, the working tier, people who could touch the veil and run the rites. They sat a little straighter, and their registers were open to the centre like taps. Across the ring a young woman in a school cardigan carried something inside her. It was folded in her like a letter in an envelope, quiet and settled. It had not been forced in. It had been placed there, and she had said yes. Gin's phrase for it came back exactly. Mutual-agreement possession. A spirit is put into a willing medium to make her stronger, in the service of the centre. She glowed with it. She was stronger than she had ever been in her life, and every bit of that strength pointed at the woman in grey.

Two places further round sat something worse. Two men, one of them in the reflective vest of a Grid courier. Their faces were present and still, and nobody was quite at home behind them. Something small and wrong looked out instead. Rei's register flinched away from them. These had been mourners once. Grief by grief the circle had emptied them. Into the empty places it had poured lesser things, stray spirits, minor demons, small hungers that did what they were told. They were hollowed. They were vessels now. Rei looked at the courier's vest and wondered how many doors in the city it could walk through without anyone asking a question. This was not only a congregation. It was an army, built one grief at a time.

Thirty-five private losses, gathered into one room and tuned to one note. The woman at the centre was the lens that focused them. And the relief on every face was real. It was the realest thing in the room. To be relieved of grief is a mercy, and each of them had truly been shown mercy.

Rei made himself follow the current to where it went. It was the only question that mattered, and he already half knew the answer. The harvested thinness did not stay here. It was being drawn away, east and down, toward the old flooded ground in Kita where he had felt the membrane scratched on purpose. It was being drawn toward the held breath before the window breaks. The circle and the drained pool where Kaito preached were one operation with two mouths. Gin's ledger bound the grateful, one careful favour at a time. Kaito's sermons tore at the wall from outside. And this room gathered the city's grief into a battery, and the thing in the woman drew it down. The horror was not that these people had been tricked. The horror was that they had been helped, and that their being helped was fuel.

The man from Sumida knelt three seats to his left. When Rei let his gift brush him, he felt the knot the ledger had described. He felt the soothed grief and the leash of gratitude. Here in the circle it was doubled. The Healer's mercy and the Far-Shore's harvest had both passed through this man, and he no longer remembered who he had been before either of them. He turned his head, mild and kind, and asked if Rei had also lost someone in the water. His face was so open and so free of pain that Rei understood how cruel his next thought was. To save this room, he might have to give grief back to people who would rather die than carry it again.

blocks.cap: Fukai Rinka, and the thing called Kishin behind her face

blocks.p: When she finally opened her eyes, the congregation breathed out together. It was a long, soft sound, like a room of sleepers turning over. Several of them swayed where they knelt, suddenly tired, the way people are tired after being carried a long way and gently set down. She looked at Rei across the ring, and for one clear second she was only a woman. Close to forty. Kind around the mouth. A teacher's patience in the set of her shoulders, a few grey hairs left in on purpose. The kind of person who would remember a stranger's name and ask after his mother.

Rei felt the trap in that clear second even while it worked on him. The thing wearing her was letting him see the host on purpose. It was like a card player who shows one honest card so the table will trust the rest of the hand.

He knew the name. It was in the CVD copies Gin kept in a drawer at the flat. Fukai Rinka. A registered clairsentient, thirty-eight years old, gentle and good at her work, which was exactly how it had found her. Her file was old, and the last line in it said alive. That was true of the body. Something had come for her in 2012, and it had not taken her the screaming way. A kishin is not a possessor that fights for the wheel. It is a resident. It moves in and turns the lights out one by one.

Rei reached under the teacher with his sight, the way he had reached into the man from Sumida. He expected to find two presences. In the man from Sumida there had been a person and a leash. In Rinka there was only one thing. The woman was gone. In the ring they called her Kanna-sensei, the way people call a thing teacher when it has taught them to feel better. And under the teacher, patient and huge and not bothering to pretend, was the one the Grid filed under a single word. Kishin.

At her throat, on a cord, hung a small grey river stone. It was smooth and plain, the kind of stone a child puts in a pocket on a beach. Rei's sight touched it, and he expected an anchor, the grounding object a practitioner keeps to find the way back to themselves. It was not one. It hummed with Rinka's last true signal, warm and human and frightened. Anyone who read this woman would find the stone first. They would feel the gentle clairsentient still in there, and they would reach in to save her. It was bait. Rei pulled his sight back as if from a hot pan. Across the ring the kind mouth smiled very slightly, because it had felt him touch it.

Here Kishin did not bother with the sermon it preached through Kaito in the drained pool. It did not hide behind mercy the way the Healer did. It simply let Rei feel its appetite, plainly, the way a person feels cold air rising from a deep well. And it wanted him to understand one fact. It was older than the politics of the seat-holders, older than the plan for the membrane, and it meant to sit above all of them. Every grief that arrived in this room fed it toward that crown. To Kishin, the Healer was a thief at the same harvest. And Rei was the most interesting thing to come up the humming stairs in months. He was Yushiro's anchor, the one person walking toward Gin instead of away. He was grief that had not yet been spent.

She lifted the iron pot beside her, the one that had been keeping warm the whole time, and poured a second cup. She did it as though this conversation had been planned. As though Rei's name had been written in a book of hers, the way the favours were written in his brother's. She did not quite say drink the tea. The kindness in it was real, and the bill in it was real, and both being real at once was the whole nature of the thing. Somewhere east and down, the battery this room had spent the evening charging was waiting to be drawn on. The woman pouring his tea was the only person in Tokyo who knew who was drawing it. She would tell him, warmly. The price was one she had not named yet, and he would not see it until it had already been paid.
